q: Skin itching and hives alone, without breathing trouble or low pressure, is treated as:
choices: distributive shock needing rapid transport only
asthma flare needing a bag-valve mask first
mild allergic reaction without epinephrine
anaphylaxis requiring immediate epinephrine
why: Skin-only allergy is mild; do not give Epi until a second system appears.

q: Adult epinephrine auto-injector dose for anaphylaxis is:
choices: 1 mg subcutaneous
0.15 mg intramuscular
0.5 mg intravenous
0.3 mg intramuscular
why: Adult Epi is 0.3 mg IM; child dose is 0.15 mg IM.

q: A retained honeybee stinger should be removed by:
choices: scraping with a firm card edge
grasping with tweezers and pulling straight out
squeezing the site until the stinger pops free
leaving it until the hospital can dig it out
why: Scrape with a credit card; tweezers squeeze more venom in.

q: Anaphylactic shock is classified as which shock type:
choices: obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax
distributive shock from wide-open vessels
cardiogenic shock from weak pump output
hypovolemic shock from blood loss
why: Anaphylaxis is distributive shock, same group as septic and neurogenic.

q: Safe senses for poison-scene clues are:
choices: sight and sound only
smell and touch only
touch and taste only
taste and smell only
why: Sight and sound are safe; smell, touch, and taste are not.

q: Powder chemical on skin is cleaned by:
choices: wiping with alcohol, then a dry sterile dressing
brushing powder off, then flushing 15–20 minutes
covering with occlusive plastic until hazmat arrives
flushing with water for five minutes first
why: Brush powder first, then flush 15–20 minutes; five minutes is wrong.

q: Naloxone reverses which toxidrome class:
choices: stimulant and cocaine uppers
opioid respiratory depression only
barbiturate and anticholinergic toxidromes
alcohol and benzodiazepine downers
why: Narcan works only on opioids; it does nothing for alcohol, benzos, or barbs.

q: After naloxone wakes a refusing opioid patient, transport is pushed because:
choices: naloxone permanently blocks opioid receptors for days
naloxone wears off faster than opioid still onboard
naloxone converts the opioid into a stimulant toxidrome
naloxone lasts longer than most street opioids
why: Narcan wears off faster than the opioid; they can go out again in about 30 minutes.

q: Which toxidrome matches hot as a hare, dry as a bone, and mad as a hatter?
choices: Opioid overdose
Botulism from bad canned food
Anticholinergic exposure
Cholinergic / nerve-agent exposure
why: Anticholinergic: hot/blind/dry/red/mad; cholinergic is SLUDGE/DUMBELS.

q: Botulism from bad home-canned food classically causes:
choices: top-to-bottom paralysis that hits breathing muscles
immediate pinpoint pupils reversed by naloxone
stimulant stroke from very high blood pressure
rotten-egg odor followed by pulmonary edema alone
why: Botulism = top-to-bottom paralysis; kills breathing muscles; ABCs/BVM.

q: On a possible behavioral call, the first assessment priority is:
choices: immediate soft restraints before any history
labeling the problem as psychiatric only
chemical sedation before airway and breathing care
a full medical check for hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or head injury
why: Do not start with “just psych”; rule out low oxygen, low sugar, or head injury.

q: Platinum 10 minutes for trauma means time from:
choices: first IV start until blood products arrive
dispatch until the trauma surgeon opens
arrival on scene until wheels rolling
injury until the first hospital CT scan
why: Platinum 10 = arrival on scene to wheels rolling toward a trauma center.

q: In the three collisions of a car crash, the main field life threat is:
choices: the body striking the passenger compartment
the airbag deploying into the face and chest
organs continuing forward and shearing inside
the vehicle stopping against another object
why: Collision 3 (organs) is the life threat — aorta, renal, and gut vessel shear.

q: Significant fall height cue for an adult is about:
choices: 40 feet only when landing on the feet
20 feet, or more than 2–3 times height for kids
10 feet onto carpet
5 feet onto soft grass
why: Grade falls by height; 20 feet (or >2–3× height for kids) is the height cue.

q: On XABCs for major trauma, the X means:
choices: exit strategy before cervical immobilization
x-ray clearance before any oxygen
extra help before gloves and scene safety
exsanguinating outside bleed before airway
why: X = huge outside bleed BEFORE airway; EMS does not carry blood.

q: All external bleeding control begins with:
choices: elevation and ice for every limb
a tourniquet high and tight
wound packing with clotting gauze
direct pressure on the wound
why: Start every bleed with direct pressure; pressure dressing if that works.

q: Groin or just-inside-shoulder arterial bleed that cannot take a tourniquet above it needs:
choices: RICE only until the hospital
a CAT twisted until it feels tight
wound packing with clotting gauze
a neck-style circumferential wrap
why: Junctional sites get packing; arms and legs get a tourniquet.

q: Eviscerated bowel dressing order is:
choices: hemostatic powder only, then a tourniquet strap
moist sterile dressing on organs, then occlusive over
push organs back in, then a pressure bandage
dry sterile gauze, then tape all four sides
why: Do not push guts in; moist sterile on organs, then plastic/occlusive over.

q: Crush syndrome time threshold before lifting a trapped limb is about:
choices: 2 hours of heavy force
30 minutes of heavy force
12 or more hours of light force
4 or more hours of heavy force
why: Crush syndrome = crush lasting 4+ hours; TQ the limb BEFORE they lift.

q: Compartment syndrome is best described as:
choices: an internal tourniquet that takes about 6–12 hours
instant paralysis the moment a limb is crushed
a scalp bruise that kills in under five seconds
air bubbles from blast primary wave in the blood
why: Compartment = squeeze from inside; book about 6–12 hours, not minutes.

q: Open sucking chest wound dressing should be:
choices: moist sterile only with no plastic cover
dry sterile gauze taped on all four sides
a bulky sandbag strapped over the flail segment
occlusive plastic taped on three sides to vent
why: Open chest gets occlusive; tape 3 sides so extra air can burp out.

q: On face or head trauma, the preferred airway adjunct rule is:
choices: oropharyngeal airway is banned after any face hit
any NPA is fine if the skull feels cracked
no NPA; use jaw thrust; OPA only if no gag
nasopharyngeal airway is preferred over jaw thrust
why: No NPA on face/head trauma; jaw thrust; OPA OK if no gag.

q: Chemical burn to the eye is treated by:
choices: pressing firmly on the globe then covering one eye
moist dressings only with lids left closed
contacts out, lids forced open, flush inside to outside ≥20 minutes
dunking the whole face in a basin for five minutes
why: Chemical still burns: contacts out, force lids, flush ≥20 minutes inside→out.

q: Epistaxis positioning for a sitting patient is:
choices: ice only on the forehead with no pinch
pack both nostrils and lie fully flat
pinch the nose and lean the head forward
pinch the nose and lean the head backward
why: Pinch and lean FORWARD; head back dumps blood into the throat.

q: Penetrating neck vessel bleed dressing rule is:
choices: tourniquet high around the entire neck
dry gauze only with a tight circumferential collar
squeeze both carotids until bleeding slows
pressure on one side; wrap under the opposite armpit; occlusive on top
why: One-side pressure, under opposite armpit, plastic to keep air out; never full circle.

q: Trauma with slow heart rate and HIGH blood pressure suggests:
choices: hypovolemic shock from uncontrolled bleeding
distributive shock from anaphylaxis alone
Cushing response from rising intracranial pressure
neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury
why: Slow heart + HIGH BP = head pressure (Cushing’s); slow + LOW BP = spinal/neurogenic.

q: After blunt head trauma, blood pressure is 200/90, the pulse is slow, and breathing is irregular. Which pattern is this?
choices: Cushing’s triad from rising pressure in the head
Compensated hemorrhagic shock from blood loss
Neurogenic shock from a spinal cord injury
Beck’s triad from cardiac tamponade
why: Cushing’s = high wide BP, bradycardia, irregular breathing; do not give nitro.

q: Epidural intracranial bleed classic pattern is:
choices: sudden worst headache without any trauma story
lucid interval — down, then up, then down again
slow venous bleed delayed for days in older adults
normal CT with no loss of consciousness ever
why: Epidural (artery, fast) = lucid interval; subdural is slow venous/delayed.

q: Which set of findings points to a basilar skull fracture?
choices: Raccoon eyes, Battle’s sign behind the ear, and CSF from the nose or ear
Paradoxical motion of one chest segment and crackles in both lungs
Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, and a response to naloxone
Kehr shoulder pain plus a pulsating mass in the belly
why: Basilar = raccoon eyes, Battle’s (mastoid), CSF from nose or ear.

q: A helmet should be removed when:
choices: the patient walked after the wreck and denies pain
full-face design blocks airway or the head rattles inside
it fits snug and airway care is still possible
the crash looked significant even with perfect fit
why: Remove if full-face blocks airway, head rattles, arrest, or cannot immobilize with it.

q: Spinal board indication after trauma includes:
choices: isolated finger fracture with normal neurologic exam
walking around after the wreck with no complaints
any car crash regardless of exam findings
unconsciousness, numbness or paralysis, or neck/back pain
why: Board for unconscious, numb/paralyzed, neck/back pain, or distrust — not just walking MOI.

q: Tension pneumothorax versus hemothorax is told apart mainly by:
choices: trachea pulled toward the quiet side in hemothorax
crackles throughout the flooded lung fields
narrow pulse pressure present only in hemothorax
neck veins — fat/JVD with tension, flat with hemo
why: Both quiet one side + shock; fat veins = air/tension, flat veins = bled-out hemo.

q: Cardiac tamponade versus tension pneumothorax: tamponade typically shows:
choices: two good lungs and a narrow pulse pressure
paradoxical flail segment moving the wrong way
flat neck veins from massive blood loss alone
quiet lung on one side and trachea pushed away
why: Both shock + JVD; tamponade has two good lungs and narrow pulse pressure.

q: Current flail chest field care is:
choices: ABCs, oxygen, shock care, and rapid transport
tape a bulky dressing and sandbags on the segment
CPAP for every pulmonary contusion under flail
needle decompression by every EMT on scene
why: Do not tape bulky dressings or sandbags; ABCs, O2, shock care, go.

q: A child who drops after a baseball to the chest needs:
choices: high-flow oxygen only while awaiting a rhythm strip
nitroglycerin to drop a wide Cushing pulse pressure
three-sided chest seal on the impact site first
CPR and AED for suspected commotio cordis / V-fib
why: Commotio cordis → V-fib; classic kid baseball; CPR + AED.

q: Which nerve roots keep the diaphragm alive (phrenic nerve)?
choices: The first three thoracic roots
C3 through C5
L1, L2, and L3 in a straight list
Only C1 and C2 at the skull base
why: Phrenic = C3–C5; cord cut above C5 → they do not breathe.

q: Pulse pressure pattern for rising intracranial pressure is:
choices: equal systolic and diastolic from the start
high and wide, for example 200/90
falling systolic with rising diastolic only
narrow and low like tamponade numbers
why: Cushing/ICP = high and WIDE pulse pressure; tamponade is narrow and low.

q: Solid abdominal organs mainly cause early:
choices: septic shock within four minutes of injury
supine hypotensive syndrome in every adult
hemorrhagic shock from bleeding
peritonitis from spilled bile and stool
why: Solid organs (liver, spleen, kidney, pancreas) bleed; hollow organs spill and irritate later.

q: Flank trauma word always points first to the:
choices: kidney in the back compartment
appendix in the right lower quadrant
spleen filtering old red cells up front
gallbladder under the right lower ribs
why: Flank = kidney always; Gray Turner flank bruise = back-compartment blood (late).

q: Second-half pregnancy trauma transport position is:
choices: right side with legs elevated above the heart
fully supine to protect the spine
left side to avoid supine hypotensive syndrome
prone with a board under the gravid uterus
why: Left side in second half; flat supine lets uterus sandwich aorta/vena cava.

q: A badly smashed pelvis can dump about:
choices: 200 mL, a minor soft-tissue loss
nothing until bruising shows around the navel
the entire 6 liters into the chest only
2 or more liters, about a third of the blood tank
why: Bad pelvis break can dump 2+ liters of about 6 — a third of the tank.

q: Abdominal exam order after look is:
choices: skip palpation if the belt mark looks minor
check for a normal pulse at a pulsating mass
push all four quadrants with the hurt quadrant last
push the sore quadrant first, then the others
why: Hurt quadrant LAST; poking sore first lights up the whole belly.

q: Vaginal bleeding field dressing is:
choices: moist sterile only because genitals never get dry
pack the vagina with clotting gauze tightly
pad on the outside, save pads, do not pack
occlusive plastic sealed on all four sides
why: Any blood → dry sterile; vaginal pad outside, never pack, save pads for the hospital.

q: Non-rebreather oxygen flow must be set to:
choices: 2–6 L/min from the start
0.5 L/min as a maintenance rate
20–25 L/min only after the bag fills
10–15 L/min from the start
why: NRB is 10–15 L/min; below 10 acts like a straw and restricts breathing.

q: Adult BVM ventilation rate for a patient not breathing is:
choices: 1 breath every 3 seconds
1 breath every 6 seconds
1 breath every 15 seconds
2 breaths every 5 seconds
why: BVM: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min); squeeze about 1 second until chest rises.

q: Maximum suction time in the adult airway skill is:
choices: 5 seconds
20 seconds
10 seconds
30 seconds
why: Suction no more than 10 seconds; same 10-second cap for pulse+breathing check.

q: A full oxygen tank gauge reading is about:
choices: 2000 PSI
1000 PSI
500 PSI
3500 PSI
why: Full tank is about 2000 PSI; listen for a hiss from a dead brass washer leak.

q: When seating the regulator on an O2 tank, the first step is:
choices: seat the two pins in the two holes, then screw it down at a right angle
screw it down tilted, then seat the pins
set flow to 15 L/min before cracking the tank
open the tank fully before the regulator touches
why: Pins go in first, then screw down; tilted means not seated.

q: Suction catheter technique after measuring mouth-corner to earlobe is:
choices: insert with suction OFF, suction ON while withdrawing in a circle
leave suction ON the whole time the tip sits deep
insert with suction ON, then pull straight out dry
measure nose to earlobe, then suction for 20 seconds
why: Insert OFF; suction ON coming out in a circle; stop by 10 seconds.

q: OPA insertion after measuring corner of mouth to earlobe is:
choices: insert sideways, then twist 90 degrees into place
insert upside down and leave it without twisting
place only after the BVM has already failed twice
force past a strong gag to guarantee an open airway
why: Measure corner-of-mouth to earlobe; insert sideways; twist 90°; needs no gag.
